docs.title: Block 7: Read grid
docs.text:
This function is the procedural spine of the example. The following blocks fill in the mesh, equation objects, material model, boundary data, outputs, and simulator call that this function orchestrates.

def run(case_name):
    # Read grid
    grid_path = os.path.join("..", "..", "..", "grids", "cube")
    grid = sf.GridHandlerGMSH("geom", grid_path)

docs.title: Block 8: Define output folder
docs.text:
This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    # Define output folder
    output_folder = os.path.join("output", f"case_{case_name}")

docs.title: Block 9: Define momentum equation
docs.text:
The displacement-based momentum equation is enough for this case. It creates vector displacement unknowns and element-wise stress/strain storage, then later receives the material model, body force, and boundary-condition handler.

    # Define momentum equation
    mom_eq = sf.LinearMomentum(grid, theta=0.0)

docs.title: Block 10: Define solver
docs.text:
The mechanical linear system is handed to PETSc. GMRES is used for the momentum formulations because mixed forms, stabilization, and history-dependent tangents can make the assembled system less friendly to simple symmetric solvers.

    # Define solver
    mom_solver = PETSc.KSP().create(grid.mesh.comm)
    mom_solver.setType("gmres")
    mom_solver.getPC().setType("asm")
    mom_solver.setTolerances(rtol=1e-12, max_it=100)
    mom_eq.set_solver(mom_solver)

docs.title: Block 11: Define material properties
docs.text:
Material is the central container for element-wise properties and constitutive mechanisms. The equation object later asks this container for stiffness, density, creep operators, thermal expansion, and thermal transport data.

    # Define material properties
    mat = sf.Material(mom_eq.n_elems)

docs.title: Block 12: Set material density
docs.text:
The density vector is stored in the Material object. Mechanics uses it when building body forces, while thermal examples keep it together with heat capacity for the transient heat-storage term.

    # Set material density
    salt_density = 2169.11
    rho = salt_density*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_density(rho)

docs.title: Block 13: Constitutive model
docs.text:
The Spring element supplies the isotropic elastic stiffness matrix used as the backbone of the mechanical model. Other inelastic mechanisms evolve around this elastic response.

    # Constitutive model
    E0 = 24.35 * GPa*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    nu0 = 0.18 * to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    spring_0 = sf.Spring(E0, nu0, "spring")

docs.title: Block 14: Create creep (A,n)
docs.text:
DislocationCreep adds a temperature- and stress-dependent salt-creep mechanism. The parameters A, Q, and n define the Arrhenius-type power law used to update non-elastic strain rates inside the simulator loop.

    # Create creep (A,n)
    A = 4.51e-33 * to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    Q = 104747.93 * to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    n = 5.5 * to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    creep_0 = sf.DislocationCreep(A, Q, n, "creep_0")

docs.title: Block 15: Create constitutive model
docs.text:
These calls register elastic stiffness, history-dependent inelastic mechanisms with the Material container. Registration order matters because the simulator loops over these lists when assembling tangents and updating internal variables.

    # Create constitutive model
    mat.add_to_elastic(spring_0)
    if case_name == "creep":
        mat.add_to_non_elastic(creep_0)

docs.title: Block 16: Set constitutive model
docs.text:
Attaching the material to the momentum equation initializes stiffness-related fields and makes the constitutive mechanisms available to the mechanical solver.

    # Set constitutive model
    mom_eq.set_material(mat)

docs.title: Block 17: Set body forces
docs.text:
The gravity vector serves two purposes in mechanics: it builds the volume body-force term through density, and it is passed to pressure boundary objects so hydrostatic variation has the correct vertical sign.

    # Set body forces
    g = -9.81
    # g = 0.0
    g_vec = [0.0, 0.0, g]
    mom_eq.build_body_force(g_vec)

docs.title: Block 18: Set initial temperature field
docs.text:
The temperature arrays define the reference and current thermal state used by temperature-dependent mechanical mechanisms.

    # Set initial temperature field
    T0_field = 326 * to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    mom_eq.set_T0(T0_field)
    mom_eq.set_T(T0_field)

docs.title: Block 19: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
A parabolic time controller is chosen to distribute a fixed number of time levels nonuniformly between the initial and final times. SafeInCave stores these times internally in seconds, so the examples can be written in hours, days, or years while the solvers use consistent units.

    tc_eq = sf.TimeControllerParabolic(n_time_steps=20,
                                        initial_time=0.0,
                                        final_time=1,
                                        time_unit="day")

docs.title: Block 20: Equilibrium Boundary Conditions
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    # -------------------------
    # Equilibrium Boundary Conditions
    # -------------------------
    bc_bottom = momBC.DirichletBC(
        boundary_name="BOTTOM",
        component=2,
        values=[0.0, 0.0],
        time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final]
    )
    bc_west = momBC.DirichletBC(
        boundary_name="WEST",
        component=0,
        values=[0.0, 0.0],
        time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final]
    )
    bc_east = momBC.DirichletBC(
        boundary_name="EAST",
        component=0,
        values=[0.0, 0.0],
        time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final]
    )
    bc_south = momBC.DirichletBC(
        boundary_name="south",
        component=1,
        values=[0.0, 0.0],
        time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final]
    )
    bc_north = momBC.DirichletBC(
        boundary_name="north",
        component=1,
        values=[0.0, 0.0],
        time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final]
    )

docs.title: Block 21: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    bc_equilibrium = momBC.BcHandler(mom_eq)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_bottom)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_west)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_east)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_south)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_north)

The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    output_mom = sf.SaveFields(mom_eq)

    output_mom.add_output_field("u", "Displacement (m)")

docs.title: Block 2: Read grid
docs.text:
This function is the procedural spine of the example. The following blocks fill in the mesh, equation objects, material model, boundary data, outputs, and simulator call that this function orchestrates.

def main():
    # Read grid
    grid_path = os.path.join("..", "..", "..", "grids", "cube")

docs.title: Block 3: Define output folder
docs.text:
This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    output_folder = os.path.join("output", "case_0")

docs.title: Block 4: Time settings for equilibrium stage
docs.text:
A parabolic time controller is chosen to distribute a fixed number of time levels nonuniformly between the initial and final times. SafeInCave stores these times internally in seconds, so the examples can be written in hours, days, or years while the solvers use consistent units.

    # Time settings for equilibrium stage
    t_control = sf.TimeControllerParabolic(n_time_steps=50, initial_time=0.0, final_time=5, time_unit="day")

docs.title: Block 5: Define equation
docs.text:
HeatDiffusion allocates the scalar temperature space, cell-wise material fields, UFL measures, and temperature storage used by the thermal solve. The example creates it before assigning material properties because set_material copies those properties into DG0 finite-element fields.

    # Define equation
    heat_eq = sf.HeatDiffusion(grid)

docs.title: Block 6: Define solver
docs.text:
The thermal linear system is solved with PETSc. Conjugate gradients match the symmetric diffusion operator, and the additive Schwarz preconditioner keeps the setup usable in both serial and parallel runs.

    # Define solver
    solver_heat = PETSc.KSP().create(grid.mesh.comm)
    solver_heat.setType("cg")
    solver_heat.getPC().setType("asm")
    solver_heat.setTolerances(rtol=1e-12, max_it=100)
    heat_eq.set_solver(solver_heat)

docs.title: Block 7: Build material properties
docs.text:
Material is the central container for element-wise properties and constitutive mechanisms. The equation object later asks this container for stiffness, density, creep operators, thermal expansion, and thermal transport data.

    # Build material properties
    mat = sf.Material(heat_eq.n_elems)

docs.title: Block 8: Set material density
docs.text:
The density vector is stored in the Material object. Mechanics uses it when building body forces, while thermal examples keep it together with heat capacity for the transient heat-storage term.

    # Set material density
    rho = 2000.0*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_density(rho)

docs.title: Block 9: Set specific heat capacity
docs.text:
Specific heat capacity controls thermal inertia. SafeInCave stores it on the material and copies it into a DG0 field inside HeatDiffusion, where it multiplies the transient temperature term.

    # Set specific heat capacity
    cp = 850*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_specific_heat_capacity(cp)

docs.title: Block 10: Set thermal conductivity
docs.text:
Thermal conductivity sets the strength of the diffusion operator. Defining it per element keeps the example ready for heterogeneous thermal properties even when the current values are uniform.

    # Set thermal conductivity
    k = 7*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_thermal_conductivity(k)

docs.title: Block 11: Set material properties to heat_equation
docs.text:
Attaching the material to HeatDiffusion copies conductivity, density, and heat capacity into finite-element fields used by the thermal variational form.

    # Set material properties to heat_equation
    heat_eq.set_material(mat)

    nt = len(time_values)

docs.text:
This Dirichlet condition fixes temperature on a named boundary. The values are time-interpolated by the heat BcHandler, which turns the user schedule into DOLFINx essential boundary conditions at each step.

    bc_east = heatBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name = "EAST",
                            values = [273, 273],
                            time_values = [t_control.t_initial, t_control.t_final])

docs.title: Block 14: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The Robin condition represents convective heat transfer between the rock boundary and a fluid temperature history. SafeInCave contributes both the boundary stiffness term and the ambient-temperature load term during heat assembly.

    bc_west = heatBC.RobinBC(boundary_name = "WEST",
                            values = [273, 273],
                            h = 5.0,
                            time_values = [t_control.t_initial, t_control.t_final])

The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_west)

docs.title: Main Functions
docs.text:
• safeincave.GridHandlerGMSH: loads the cube mesh from grids/cube.
  • safeincave.HeatDiffusion: defines the heat diffusion equation.
  • safeincave.Material: stores density, specific heat capacity, and thermal conductivity.
  • safeincave.HeatBC.DirichletBC: prescribes a fixed temperature on the EAST boundary.
  • safeincave.HeatBC.RobinBC: applies convective heat exchange on the WEST boundary.
  • safeincave.TimeControllerParabolic: creates the parabolic time discretization.
  • safeincave.SaveFields: saves the temperature field.
  • safeincave.Simulator_T: runs the thermal simulation.

docs.title: Running the Example
docs.text:
From the repository root, run:

cd examples/thermal/1_cube
python main.py

The simulation writes temperature results to output/case_0. To inspect the results with the provided plotting script, run:

python plot_results.py

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: This example demonstrates the minimal workflow for a thermal SafeInCave simulation: load a mesh, define thermal material properties, assign thermal boundary conditions, save temperature, and run Simulator_T.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This example computes heat diffusion around a cavern over a five-year period. The model uses a geothermal gradient as the initial condition, insulated lateral boundaries, and a convective condition at the cavern wall with a time-dependent gas temperature.

docs.title: Problem description
docs.text: This section walks through examples/thermal/2_cavern/main.py as an annotated, notebook-style listing. The code blocks follow the script in order and include all non-empty lines from main.py. Each block explains not only what the code does, but why the SafeInCave object is needed in the simulation workflow.

docs.title: Block 1: Imports and dependencies
docs.text:
The imports reveal the physics activated by this example: thermal boundary conditions, PETSc linear solvers. Loading these modules up front keeps the script explicit about which SafeInCave subsystems will be wired together.

import safeincave as sf
import safeincave.Utils as ut
import safeincave.HeatBC as heatBC
from petsc4py import PETSc
import torch as to
import os

docs.title: Block 2: Read grid
docs.text:
This function is the procedural spine of the example. The following blocks fill in the mesh, equation objects, material model, boundary data, outputs, and simulator call that this function orchestrates.

def main():
    # Read grid
    grid_path = os.path.join("..", "..", "..", "grids", "cavern_regular")
    grid = sf.GridHandlerGMSH("geom", grid_path)

docs.title: Block 3: Define output folder
docs.text:
This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    # Define output folder
    output_folder = os.path.join("output", "case_0")

docs.title: Block 4: Time settings for equilibrium stage
docs.text:
A parabolic time controller is chosen to distribute a fixed number of time levels nonuniformly between the initial and final times. SafeInCave stores these times internally in seconds, so the examples can be written in hours, days, or years while the solvers use consistent units.

    # Time settings for equilibrium stage
    t_control = sf.TimeControllerParabolic(n_time_steps=100, initial_time=0, final_time=5, time_unit="year")

docs.title: Block 5: Define equation
docs.text:
HeatDiffusion allocates the scalar temperature space, cell-wise material fields, UFL measures, and temperature storage used by the thermal solve. The example creates it before assigning material properties because set_material copies those properties into DG0 finite-element fields.

    # Define equation
    heat_eq = sf.HeatDiffusion(grid)

docs.title: Block 6: Define solver
docs.text:
The thermal linear system is solved with PETSc. Conjugate gradients match the symmetric diffusion operator, and the additive Schwarz preconditioner keeps the setup usable in both serial and parallel runs.

    # Define solver
    solver_heat = PETSc.KSP().create(grid.mesh.comm)
    solver_heat.setType("cg")
    solver_heat.getPC().setType("asm")
    solver_heat.setTolerances(rtol=1e-12, max_it=100)
    heat_eq.set_solver(solver_heat)

docs.title: Block 7: Build material properties
docs.text:
Material is the central container for element-wise properties and constitutive mechanisms. The equation object later asks this container for stiffness, density, creep operators, thermal expansion, and thermal transport data.

    # Build material properties
    mat = sf.Material(heat_eq.n_elems)

docs.title: Block 8: Set material density
docs.text:
The density vector is stored in the Material object. Mechanics uses it when building body forces, while thermal examples keep it together with heat capacity for the transient heat-storage term.

    # Set material density
    rho = 2000.0*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_density(rho)

docs.title: Block 9: Set specific heat capacity
docs.text:
Specific heat capacity controls thermal inertia. SafeInCave stores it on the material and copies it into a DG0 field inside HeatDiffusion, where it multiplies the transient temperature term.

    # Set specific heat capacity
    cp = 850*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_specific_heat_capacity(cp)

docs.title: Block 10: Set thermal conductivity
docs.text:
Thermal conductivity sets the strength of the diffusion operator. Defining it per element keeps the example ready for heterogeneous thermal properties even when the current values are uniform.

    # Set thermal conductivity
    k = 7*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_thermal_conductivity(k)

docs.title: Block 11: Set material properties to heat_equation
docs.text:
Attaching the material to HeatDiffusion copies conductivity, density, and heat capacity into finite-element fields used by the thermal variational form.

    # Set material properties to heat_equation
    heat_eq.set_material(mat)

docs.title: Block 12: Define boundary conditions for heat diffusion
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Define boundary conditions for heat diffusion
    time_values = [t_control.t_initial, t_control.t_final]
    nt = len(time_values)

docs.title: Block 13: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    km = 1000
    dTdZ = 27/km
    T_top = 273 + 20
    h_conv = 5.0

docs.title: Block 14: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    bc_handler = heatBC.BcHandler(heat_eq)

docs.title: Block 15: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
This Dirichlet condition fixes temperature on a named boundary. The values are time-interpolated by the heat BcHandler, which turns the user schedule into DOLFINx essential boundary conditions at each step.

    bc_top = heatBC.DirichletBC("Top", nt*[T_top], time_values)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_top)

docs.title: Block 16: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
This Neumann condition prescribes heat flux. A geothermal gradient at the bottom supplies heat from depth, while zero flux on side boundaries idealizes lateral insulation.

    bc_bottom = heatBC.NeumannBC("Bottom", nt*[dTdZ], time_values)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_bottom)

docs.title: Block 17: Continuation of the script

    bc_east = heatBC.NeumannBC("East", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_east)

    bc_west = heatBC.NeumannBC("West", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_west)

docs.text:
This Neumann condition prescribes heat flux. A geothermal gradient at the bottom supplies heat from depth, while zero flux on side boundaries idealizes lateral insulation.

    bc_south = heatBC.NeumannBC("South", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_south)

docs.text:
This Neumann condition prescribes heat flux. A geothermal gradient at the bottom supplies heat from depth, while zero flux on side boundaries idealizes lateral insulation.

    bc_north = heatBC.NeumannBC("North", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_north)

docs.title: Block 21: Gas temperature schedule over time
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Gas temperature schedule over time
    #      T(K) ^
    #           |
    #       310 |_ _ _  ___________
    #           |      /|          |
    #           |    /
    #           |  /    |          |
    #       303 |/
    #           |       |          |
    #           +-------+----------+-----> Time
    #          t_0    t_f/2       t_f

docs.title: Block 22: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The Robin condition represents convective heat transfer between the rock boundary and a fluid temperature history. SafeInCave contributes both the boundary stiffness term and the ambient-temperature load term during heat assembly.

    bc_cavern = heatBC.RobinBC(
                                boundary_name = "Cavern",
                                values = [303, 310, 310],
                                h = h_conv,
                                time_values = [t_control.t_initial, t_control.t_final/2, t_control.t_final]
    )
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_cavern)

docs.title: Block 23: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    heat_eq.set_boundary_conditions(bc_handler)

docs.title: Block 24: Set initial temperature field
docs.text:
The initial temperature initializes both current and previous thermal states inside HeatDiffusion. Without this step the transient solve would not have a physically meaningful starting field.

    # Set initial temperature field
    fun = lambda x, y, z: T_top - dTdZ*(z - 660)
    T0_field = ut.create_field_nodes(heat_eq.grid, fun)
    heat_eq.set_initial_T(T0_field)

docs.title: Block 25: Create output handlers
docs.text:
This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    # Create output handlers
    output_heat = sf.SaveFields(heat_eq)
    output_heat.set_output_folder(output_folder)
    output_heat.add_output_field("T", "Temperature (K)")
    outputs = [output_heat]

docs.title: Block 26: Define simulator
docs.text:
Simulator_T advances the heat equation and writes the thermal fields. It is the appropriate driver when the example is only concerned with temperature evolution.

    # Define simulator
    sim = sf.Simulator_T(heat_eq, t_control, outputs, True)
    sim.run()

docs.title: Block 27: Script entry point
docs.text:
The entry-point guard keeps the file importable while still running main() when executed as a script.

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

docs.title: Main Functions
docs.text:
• safeincave.GridHandlerGMSH: reads the cavern_regular mesh and boundary tags.
  • safeincave.HeatDiffusion: defines the thermal problem.
  • safeincave.Material: assigns density, heat capacity, and thermal conductivity.
  • safeincave.Utils.create_field_nodes: builds the initial geothermal temperature field.
  • safeincave.HeatBC.DirichletBC: fixes the temperature at the top boundary.
  • safeincave.HeatBC.NeumannBC: applies the basal geothermal gradient and no-flux side boundaries.
  • safeincave.HeatBC.RobinBC: models heat transfer between the cavern wall and cavern gas.
  • safeincave.Simulator_T: advances the transient thermal problem.

docs.text: This example shows how to impose geological thermal conditions and a cavern-wall heat transfer law. It is a useful starting point for thermal initialization before coupled thermomechanical cavern analyses.

docs.title: Block 1: Imports and dependencies
docs.text:
The example stays at the lumped-fluid level, so it imports numerical arrays, plotting tools, and CavernThermodynamics rather than finite-element classes. CavernThermodynamics is the SafeInCave wrapper around CoolProp and the nonlinear energy/mass balance used to advance the fluid state.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from safeincave.Thermodynamics import CavernThermodynamics

docs.title: Block 3: Function apply_grey_theme
docs.text:
This is a plotting convenience, not a modeling operation. It gives all thermodynamic plots a common visual style so differences in pressure, temperature, or density are easier to compare.

def apply_grey_theme(fig, axes, transparent=True, grid_color="0.92", back_color='0.85'):
    fig.patch.set_facecolor("#212121ff")
    if transparent:
        fig.patch.set_alpha(0.0)
    for ax in axes:
        if ax != None:
            ax.grid(True, color=grid_color)
            ax.set_axisbelow(True)
            ax.spines['bottom'].set_color('black')
            ax.spines['top'].set_color('black')
            ax.spines['right'].set_color('black')
            ax.spines['left'].set_color('black')
            ax.tick_params(axis='x', colors='black', which='both')
            ax.tick_params(axis='y', colors='black', which='both')
            ax.yaxis.label.set_color('black')
            ax.xaxis.label.set_color('black')
            ax.set_facecolor(back_color)

docs.title: Block 4: Function volumes
docs.text:
This helper builds the imposed cavern-volume path. Changing V0 to V1 is the only physical driver in the adiabatic volume-change example.

def volumes(V_min, V_max):
    time = np.linspace(0, 100, 100)
    vol = V_min + (V_max - V_min)*time/time[-1]
    return time, vol

docs.title: Block 5: Function calculate_thermodynamics
docs.text:
This function contains the physical update loop. It creates a CavernThermodynamics object for the requested fluid, computes the initial density/internal-energy state, and repeatedly calls solve so volume change is translated into pressure, temperature, and density.

def calculate_thermodynamics(fluid_name, volumes, P_init=10*MPa, T_init=300):
    model = CavernThermodynamics(fluid_name)
    P_atm = 101325.0
    rho_init, _, _ = model.rho_u_h(P_init + P_atm, T_init)
    T, P, rho = [T_init], [P_init], [rho_init]
    for i in range(1, len(volumes)):
        P1, T1, rho1 = model.solve( dm = 0.0,
                                    Q_in = 0.0,
                                    T_in = 0.0,
                                    P0 = P[i-1] + P_atm,
                                    T0 = T[i-1],
                                    V0 = volumes[i-1],
                                    V1 = volumes[i])
        P.append(P1 - P_atm)
        T.append(T1)
        rho.append(rho1)
    return np.array(P), np.array(T), np.array(rho)

def main():

    fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.935, bottom=0.155, left=0.045, right=0.980, hspace=0.35, wspace=0.38)

docs.title: Main Functions
docs.text:
• safeincave.Thermodynamics.CavernThermodynamics: evaluates fluid thermodynamic properties and solves the closed cavern state update.
  • CavernThermodynamics.rho_u_h: computes the initial density and thermodynamic state from pressure and temperature.
  • CavernThermodynamics.solve: advances pressure, temperature, and density from the previous state and the new cavern volume.
  • volumes: creates the prescribed volume histories used by the example.
  • calculate_thermodynamics: loops over the volume history and stores pressure, temperature, and density.

docs.title: Block 4: Function heat
docs.text:
This helper creates the heat-input history. The subsequent thermodynamic loop keeps volume and mass fixed, so Q_in is the only source term changing the water state.

def heat(Q_min, Q_max):
    time = np.linspace(0, 100, 100)
    Q_list = Q_min + (Q_max - Q_min)*time/time[-1]
    return time, Q_list

docs.title: Block 5: Function calculate_thermodynamics
docs.text:
This function contains the physical update loop. It creates a CavernThermodynamics object for the requested fluid, computes the initial density/internal-energy state, and repeatedly calls solve so heat input is translated into pressure, temperature, and density.

def calculate_thermodynamics(fluid_name, Q_list, P_init=10*MPa, T_init=300):
    model = CavernThermodynamics(fluid_name)
    P_atm = 101325.0
    rho_init, _, _ = model.rho_u_h(P_init + P_atm, T_init)
    T, P, rho = [T_init], [P_init], [rho_init]
    for i in range(1, len(Q_list)):
        P1, T1, rho1 = model.solve( dm = 0.0,
                                    Q_in = Q_list[i],
                                    T_in = 0.0,
                                    P0 = P[i-1] + P_atm,
                                    T0 = T[i-1],
                                    V0 = 1,
                                    V1 = 1)
        P.append(P1 - P_atm)
        T.append(T1)
        rho.append(rho1)
    return np.array(P), np.array(T), np.array(rho)

docs.title: Block 3: Function apply_grey_theme
docs.text:
This is a plotting convenience, not a modeling operation. It gives all thermodynamic plots a common visual style so differences in pressure, temperature, or density are easier to compare.

def apply_grey_theme(fig, axes, transparent=True, grid_color="0.92", back_color='0.85'):
    fig.patch.set_facecolor("#212121ff")
    if transparent:
        fig.patch.set_alpha(0.0)
    for ax in axes:
        if ax != None:
            ax.grid(True, color=grid_color)
            ax.set_axisbelow(True)
            ax.spines['bottom'].set_color('black')
            ax.spines['top'].set_color('black')
            ax.spines['right'].set_color('black')
            ax.spines['left'].set_color('black')
            ax.tick_params(axis='x', colors='black', which='both')
            ax.tick_params(axis='y', colors='black', which='both')
            ax.yaxis.label.set_color('black')
            ax.xaxis.label.set_color('black')
            ax.set_facecolor(back_color)

docs.title: Block 4: Function mass_rate
docs.text:
This helper creates the injection or withdrawal history. Positive increments add hydrogen to the fixed-volume cavern, while negative values remove mass.

def mass_rate(M_min, M_max):
    time = np.linspace(0, 100, 100)
    dM_list = M_min + (M_max - M_min)*time/time[-1]
    return time, dM_list

docs.title: Block 5: Function calculate_thermodynamics
docs.text:
This function contains the physical update loop. It creates a CavernThermodynamics object for the requested fluid, computes the initial density/internal-energy state, and repeatedly calls solve so mass exchange is translated into pressure, temperature, and density.

def calculate_thermodynamics(fluid_name, dM_list, P_init=10*MPa, T_init=300):
    model = CavernThermodynamics(fluid_name)
    P_atm = 101325.0
    rho_init, _, _ = model.rho_u_h(P_init + P_atm, T_init)
    T, P, rho = [T_init], [P_init], [rho_init]
    for i in range(1, len(dM_list)):
        P1, T1, rho1 = model.solve( dm = dM_list[i],
                                    Q_in = 0.0,
                                    T_in = 280.0,
                                    P0 = P[i-1] + P_atm,
                                    T0 = T[i-1],
                                    V0 = 1,
                                    V1 = 1)
        P.append(P1 - P_atm)
        T.append(T1)
        rho.append(rho1)
    return np.array(P), np.array(T), np.array(rho)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This example runs a coupled thermomechanical simulation on a cube with two material regions. A cooling boundary condition produces a temperature field, and the mechanical solver computes the resulting thermoelastic stresses for three formulations: P1, P1P1, and stabilized P1P1.

docs.title: Problem description
docs.text: This section walks through examples/thermomechanics/1_cube/main.py as an annotated, notebook-style listing. The code blocks follow the script in order and include all non-empty lines from main.py. Each block explains not only what the code does, but why the SafeInCave object is needed in the simulation workflow.

docs.title: Block 1: Imports and dependencies
docs.text:
The imports reveal the physics activated by this example: mechanical boundary conditions, thermal boundary conditions, PETSc linear solvers. Loading these modules up front keeps the script explicit about which SafeInCave subsystems will be wired together.

import safeincave as sf
import safeincave.Utils as ut
import safeincave.HeatBC as heatBC
import safeincave.MomentumBC as momBC
from petsc4py import PETSc
from mpi4py import MPI
import torch as to
import os
import sys

docs.title: Block 2: Read grid
docs.text:
This function is the procedural spine of the example. The following blocks fill in the mesh, equation objects, material model, boundary data, outputs, and simulator call that this function orchestrates.

def run(formulation):
    # Read grid
    grid_path = os.path.join("..", "..", "..", "grids", "cube_regions")
    grid = sf.GridHandlerGMSH("geom", grid_path)

docs.title: Block 3: Define output folder
docs.text:
This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    # Define output folder
    output_folder = os.path.join("output", "case_0", f"{formulation}")

docs.title: Block 4: Time settings for equilibrium stage
docs.text:
A parabolic time controller is chosen to distribute a fixed number of time levels nonuniformly between the initial and final times. SafeInCave stores these times internally in seconds, so the examples can be written in hours, days, or years while the solvers use consistent units.

    # Time settings for equilibrium stage
    t_control = sf.TimeControllerParabolic(n_time_steps=100, initial_time=0.0, final_time=10, time_unit="day")

docs.title: Block 5: Define equation
docs.text:
HeatDiffusion allocates the scalar temperature space, cell-wise material fields, UFL measures, and temperature storage used by the thermal solve. The example creates it before assigning material properties because set_material copies those properties into DG0 finite-element fields.

    # Define equation
    heat_eq = sf.HeatDiffusion(grid)

docs.title: Block 6: Define solver
docs.text:
The thermal linear system is solved with PETSc. Conjugate gradients match the symmetric diffusion operator, and the additive Schwarz preconditioner keeps the setup usable in both serial and parallel runs.

    # Define solver
    solver_heat = PETSc.KSP().create(grid.mesh.comm)
    solver_heat.setType("cg")
    solver_heat.getPC().setType("asm")
    solver_heat.setTolerances(rtol=1e-12, max_it=100)
    heat_eq.set_solver(solver_heat)

docs.title: Block 7: Build material properties
docs.text:
Material is the central container for element-wise properties and constitutive mechanisms. The equation object later asks this container for stiffness, density, creep operators, thermal expansion, and thermal transport data.

    # Build material properties
    mat = sf.Material(heat_eq.n_elems)

docs.title: Block 8: Set material density
docs.text:
The density vector is stored in the Material object. Mechanics uses it when building body forces, while thermal examples keep it together with heat capacity for the transient heat-storage term.

    # Set material density
    rho = 2000.0*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_density(rho)

docs.title: Block 9: Set specific heat capacity
docs.text:
Specific heat capacity controls thermal inertia. SafeInCave stores it on the material and copies it into a DG0 field inside HeatDiffusion, where it multiplies the transient temperature term.

    # Set specific heat capacity
    cp = 850*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_specific_heat_capacity(cp)

docs.title: Block 10: Set thermal conductivity
docs.text:
Thermal conductivity sets the strength of the diffusion operator. Defining it per element keeps the example ready for heterogeneous thermal properties even when the current values are uniform.

    # Set thermal conductivity
    k = 7*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_thermal_conductivity(k)

docs.title: Block 11: Set material properties to heat_equation
docs.text:
Attaching the material to HeatDiffusion copies conductivity, density, and heat capacity into finite-element fields used by the thermal variational form.

    # Set material properties to heat_equation
    heat_eq.set_material(mat)

docs.title: Block 12: Define boundary conditions for heat diffusion
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Define boundary conditions for heat diffusion
    time_values = [t_control.t_initial, t_control.t_final]
    nt = len(time_values)

docs.title: Block 13: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
This Dirichlet condition fixes temperature on a named boundary. The values are time-interpolated by the heat BcHandler, which turns the user schedule into DOLFINx essential boundary conditions at each step.

    bc_east = heatBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name = "EAST",
                            values = nt*[273 + 1.0],
                            time_values = time_values)

docs.title: Block 14: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    bc_handler = heatBC.BcHandler(heat_eq)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_east)
    heat_eq.set_boundary_conditions(bc_handler)

docs.title: Block 15: Set initial temperature field
docs.text:
The initial temperature initializes both current and previous thermal states inside HeatDiffusion. Without this step the transient solve would not have a physically meaningful starting field.

    # Set initial temperature field
    fun = lambda x, y, z: 273 + 20
    T0_field = ut.create_field_nodes(heat_eq.grid, fun)
    heat_eq.set_initial_T(T0_field)

docs.title: Block 16: Define momentum equation
docs.text:
The mixed momentum formulation is selected when pressure-related stability or volumetric behavior matters. The stab_scaling parameter controls the pressure-stabilization contribution, while theta sets the time-integration convention used by inelastic updates.

    # Define momentum equation
    theta = 0.5
    if formulation == "P1":
        mom_eq = sf.LinearMomentum(grid, theta=theta)
    elif formulation == "P1P1":
        mom_eq = sf.LinearMomentumMixed(grid, theta=theta, stab_scaling=0.0)
    elif formulation == "P1P1_Stab":
        mom_eq = sf.LinearMomentumMixed(grid, theta=theta, stab_scaling=1.0)

docs.title: Block 17: Define solver
docs.text:
The mechanical linear system is handed to PETSc. GMRES is used for the momentum formulations because mixed forms, stabilization, and history-dependent tangents can make the assembled system less friendly to simple symmetric solvers.

    # Define solver
    mom_solver = PETSc.KSP().create(grid.mesh.comm)
    mom_solver.setType("gmres")
    mom_solver.getPC().setType("asm")
    mom_solver.setTolerances(rtol=1e-12, max_it=100)
    mom_eq.set_solver(mom_solver)

docs.title: Block 18: Constitutive model
docs.text:
The Spring element supplies the isotropic elastic stiffness matrix used as the backbone of the mechanical model. Other inelastic mechanisms evolve around this elastic response.

    # Constitutive model
    E = 102e9*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    nu = 0.3*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    spring_0 = sf.Spring(E, nu, "spring")

docs.title: Block 19: Extract region indices
docs.text:
The region-index dictionaries come from GridHandlerGMSH. They let the script assign arrays element by element, so salt, overburden, or separate cube regions can share one mesh while keeping distinct properties.

    # Extract region indices
    omega_A = grid.region_indices["OMEGA_A"]
    omega_B = grid.region_indices["OMEGA_B"]

docs.title: Block 20: Thermo-elastic element
docs.text:
The thermoelastic element converts temperature changes into thermal strain, alpha * deltaT * I. Adding it to the material is what lets heat diffusion produce mechanical stress and deformation in coupled examples.

    # Thermo-elastic element
    alpha = to.zeros(mom_eq.n_elems)
    alpha[omega_A] = 44e-6
    alpha[omega_B] = 74e-6
    # alpha = 44e-6*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    thermo = sf.Thermoelastic(alpha, "thermo")

docs.title: Block 21: Create constitutive model
docs.text:
These calls register elastic stiffness, thermal strain coupling with the Material container. Registration order matters because the simulator loops over these lists when assembling tangents and updating internal variables.

    # Create constitutive model
    mat.add_to_elastic(spring_0)
    mat.add_to_thermoelastic(thermo)

docs.title: Block 22: Set constitutive model
docs.text:
Attaching the material to the momentum equation initializes stiffness-related fields and makes the constitutive mechanisms available to the mechanical solver.

    # Set constitutive model
    mom_eq.set_material(mat)

docs.title: Block 23: Set body forces
docs.text:
The gravity vector serves two purposes in mechanics: it builds the volume body-force term through density, and it is passed to pressure boundary objects so hydrostatic variation has the correct vertical sign.

    # Set body forces
    g = -9.81
    g_vec = [0.0, 0.0, g]
    mom_eq.build_body_force(g_vec)

docs.title: Block 24: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    # Boundary conditions
    bc_west_2 = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name = "WEST",
                            component = 2,
                            values = nt*[0.0],
                            time_values = time_values)

docs.title: Block 25: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    bc_west_1 = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name = "WEST",
                            component = 1,
                            values = nt*[0.0],
                            time_values = time_values)

docs.title: Block 26: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    bc_west_0 = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name = "WEST",
                          component = 0,
                          values = nt*[0.0],
                          time_values = time_values)

docs.title: Block 27: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    bc_bottom = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name = "BOTTOM",
                          component = 2,
                          values = nt*[0.0],
                          time_values = time_values)

docs.title: Block 28: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    bc_handler = momBC.BcHandler(mom_eq)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_west_0)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_west_1)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_west_2)
    bc_handler.add_boundary_condition(bc_bottom)

The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

Simulator_TM couples heat diffusion and mechanics without solving a cavern thermodynamic model. After each heat step, element temperatures are transferred to the mechanical constitutive update.

This function is the procedural spine of the example. The following blocks fill in the mesh, equation objects, material model, boundary data, outputs, and simulator call that this function orchestrates.

docs.title: Main Functions
docs.text:
• safeincave.GridHandlerGMSH: loads the cube_regions mesh and region labels.
  • safeincave.HeatDiffusion: solves transient heat diffusion.
  • safeincave.LinearMomentum and safeincave.LinearMomentumMixed: define the mechanical formulations.
  • safeincave.Material: stores thermal and mechanical material properties.
  • safeincave.Spring and safeincave.Thermoelastic: define elastic stiffness and thermal expansion.
  • safeincave.HeatBC.DirichletBC: applies a fixed temperature boundary.
  • safeincave.MomentumBC.DirichletBC: constrains selected displacement components.
  • safeincave.Simulator_TM: runs the coupled thermal-mechanical problem.

docs.title: Running the Example
docs.text:
From the repository root, run:

cd examples/thermomechanics/1_cube
python main.py

The script runs all three mechanical formulations and writes separate result folders under output/case_0. To inspect the fields, run:

python plot_results.py

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: This example demonstrates the basic coupled workflow in SafeInCave and shows how thermal expansion coefficients can vary by mesh region. It also provides a compact comparison setup for the available mechanical formulations.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This example models a salt cavern with overburden in two stages. First, it computes a mechanical equilibrium state under geostatic loading and cavern pressure. Then it couples heat diffusion and mechanics during a 240-day operation stage with changing cavern pressure.

docs.title: Problem description
docs.text: This section walks through examples/thermomechanics/2_cavern/main.py as an annotated, notebook-style listing. The code blocks follow the script in order and include all non-empty lines from main.py. Each block explains not only what the code does, but why the SafeInCave object is needed in the simulation workflow.

docs.title: Block 1: Imports and dependencies
docs.text:
The imports reveal the physics activated by this example: mechanical boundary conditions, thermal boundary conditions, PETSc linear solvers, field sampling utilities. Loading these modules up front keeps the script explicit about which SafeInCave subsystems will be wired together.

import safeincave as sf
import safeincave.Utils as ut
from safeincave.Utils import GPa, MPa, day, hour, create_field_elems, create_field_nodes
import safeincave.HeatBC as heatBC
import safeincave.MomentumBC as momBC
from petsc4py import PETSc
from mpi4py import MPI
import os
import sys
import torch as to

docs.title: Block 2: Function get_geometry_parameters
docs.text:
This helper reads geometric constants directly from the mesh-generation file. The example uses those dimensions to derive physically meaningful pressure references, instead of hard-coding cavern roof or overburden values in several places.

def get_geometry_parameters(path_to_grid):
    f = open(os.path.join(path_to_grid, "geom.geo"), "r")
    data = f.readlines()
    ovb_thickness = float(data[10][len("ovb_thickness = "):-2])
    salt_thickness = float(data[11][len("salt_thickness = "):-2])
    hanging_wall = float(data[12][len("hanging_wall = "):-2])
    return ovb_thickness, salt_thickness, hanging_wall

docs.title: Block 3: Read grid
docs.text:
This function is the procedural spine of the example. The following blocks fill in the mesh, equation objects, material model, boundary data, outputs, and simulator call that this function orchestrates.

def run(formulation):
    # Read grid
    grid_path = os.path.join("..", "..", "..", "grids", "cavern_overburden_coarse")
    grid = sf.GridHandlerGMSH("geom", grid_path)

docs.title: Block 4: Define output folder
docs.text:
This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    # Define output folder
    output_folder = os.path.join("output", "case_0", f"{formulation}")

docs.title: Block 5: Extract region indices
docs.text:
The region-index dictionaries come from GridHandlerGMSH. They let the script assign arrays element by element, so salt, overburden, or separate cube regions can share one mesh while keeping distinct properties.

    # Extract region indices
    ind_salt = grid.region_indices["Salt"]
    ind_ovb = grid.region_indices["Overburden"]

docs.title: Block 6: Define momentum equation
docs.text:
The mixed momentum formulation is selected when pressure-related stability or volumetric behavior matters. The stab_scaling parameter controls the pressure-stabilization contribution, while theta sets the time-integration convention used by inelastic updates.

    # Define momentum equation
    theta = 0.0
    if formulation == "P1":
        mom_eq = sf.LinearMomentum(grid, theta=theta)
    elif formulation == "P1P1":
        mom_eq = sf.LinearMomentumMixed(grid, theta=theta, stab_scaling=0.0)
    elif formulation == "P1P1_Stab":
        mom_eq = sf.LinearMomentumMixed(grid, theta=theta, stab_scaling=1.0)

docs.title: Block 7: Define solver
docs.text:
The mechanical linear system is handed to PETSc. GMRES is used for the momentum formulations because mixed forms, stabilization, and history-dependent tangents can make the assembled system less friendly to simple symmetric solvers.

    # Define solver
    mom_solver = PETSc.KSP().create(grid.mesh.comm)
    mom_solver.setType("gmres")
    mom_solver.getPC().setType("asm")
    mom_solver.setTolerances(rtol=1e-12, max_it=100)
    mom_eq.set_solver(mom_solver)

docs.title: Block 8: Define material properties
docs.text:
Material is the central container for element-wise properties and constitutive mechanisms. The equation object later asks this container for stiffness, density, creep operators, thermal expansion, and thermal transport data.

    # Define material properties
    mat = sf.Material(mom_eq.n_elems)

docs.title: Block 9: Set material density
docs.text:
Density is assigned as an element-wise tensor rather than a scalar so each geological region can carry its own body-force contribution. The same vector is also available to material routines that need density-dependent quantities.

    # Set material density
    gas_density = 0.082
    salt_density = 2200
    ovb_density = 2800
    rho = to.zeros(mom_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    rho[ind_salt] = salt_density
    rho[ind_ovb] = ovb_density
    mat.set_density(rho)

docs.title: Block 10: Constitutive model
docs.text:
The spring is the elastic part of the constitutive model. Here its Young modulus and Poisson ratio are assembled as element-wise arrays, which is why different mesh regions can receive different elastic stiffness.

    # Constitutive model
    E0 = to.zeros(mom_eq.n_elems)
    E0[ind_salt] = 102*GPa
    E0[ind_ovb] = 180*GPa
    nu0 = 0.3*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    spring_0 = sf.Spring(E0, nu0, "spring")

docs.title: Block 11: Create Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic element
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Create Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic element
    # eta = 105e11*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    E1 = 10*GPa*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    nu1 = 0.32*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)

docs.title: Block 12: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The Kelvin-Voigt Viscoelastic element adds delayed, rate-dependent strain. It is included when the example needs short-term transient deformation beyond purely elastic response.

    eta = to.zeros(mom_eq.n_elems)
    eta[ind_salt] = 105e11
    eta[ind_ovb] = 105e21
    kelvin = sf.Viscoelastic(eta, E1, nu1, "kelvin")

docs.title: Block 13: Create dislocation creep
docs.text:
DislocationCreep adds a temperature- and stress-dependent salt-creep mechanism. The parameters A, Q, and n define the Arrhenius-type power law used to update non-elastic strain rates inside the simulator loop.

    # Create dislocation creep
    A = to.zeros(mom_eq.n_elems)
    A[ind_salt] = 1.9e-20
    A[ind_ovb] = 0.0
    Q = 51600*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    n = 3.0*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    creep_ds = sf.DislocationCreep(A, Q, n, "ds_creep")

docs.title: Block 14: Create pressure solution creep
docs.text:
PressureSolutionCreep represents another salt-creep pathway, controlled by stress, temperature, activation energy, and grain-size parameter d. It is combined with dislocation creep through the Material non-elastic element list.

    # Create pressure solution creep
    A = to.zeros(mom_eq.n_elems)
    A[ind_salt] = 1.29e-19
    A[ind_ovb] = 0.0
    Q = 13184*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    d = 0.01*to.ones(mom_eq.n_elems)
    creep_ps = sf.PressureSolutionCreep(A, d, Q, "ps_creep")

docs.title: Block 15: Thermo-elastic element
docs.text:
The thermoelastic element converts temperature changes into thermal strain, alpha * deltaT * I. Adding it to the material is what lets heat diffusion produce mechanical stress and deformation in coupled examples.

    # Thermo-elastic element
    alpha = to.zeros(mom_eq.n_elems)
    alpha[ind_salt] = 44e-6
    alpha[ind_ovb] = 0.0
    thermo = sf.Thermoelastic(alpha, "thermo")

docs.title: Block 16: Create constitutive model
docs.text:
These calls register elastic stiffness, history-dependent inelastic mechanisms, thermal strain coupling with the Material container. Registration order matters because the simulator loops over these lists when assembling tangents and updating internal variables.

    # Create constitutive model
    mat.add_to_elastic(spring_0)
    mat.add_to_thermoelastic(thermo)
    mat.add_to_non_elastic(kelvin)
    mat.add_to_non_elastic(creep_ds)
    mat.add_to_non_elastic(creep_ps)

docs.title: Block 17: Set constitutive model
docs.text:
Attaching the material to the momentum equation initializes stiffness-related fields and makes the constitutive mechanisms available to the mechanical solver.

    # Set constitutive model
    mom_eq.set_material(mat)

docs.title: Block 18: Set body forces
docs.text:
The gravity vector serves two purposes in mechanics: it builds the volume body-force term through density, and it is passed to pressure boundary objects so hydrostatic variation has the correct vertical sign.

    # Set body forces
    g = -9.81
    g_vec = [0.0, 0.0, g]
    mom_eq.build_body_force(g_vec)

docs.title: Block 19: Set initial temperature field
docs.text:
The temperature function is evaluated at element centroids. This is the right representation for mechanical constitutive laws because creep and thermoelastic strain are stored per element.

    # Set initial temperature field
    km = 1000
    dTdZ = 27/km
    T_top = 273 + 20
    T_field_fun = lambda x,y,z: T_top + dTdZ*(660 - z)
    T0_field = create_field_elems(grid, T_field_fun)
    mom_eq.set_T0(T0_field)
    mom_eq.set_T(T0_field)

docs.title: Block 20: Time settings for equilibrium stage
docs.text:
A parabolic time controller is chosen to distribute a fixed number of time levels nonuniformly between the initial and final times. SafeInCave stores these times internally in seconds, so the examples can be written in hours, days, or years while the solvers use consistent units.

    # Time settings for equilibrium stage
    tc_eq = sf.TimeControllerParabolic(n_time_steps=20, initial_time=0.0, final_time=10, time_unit="day")
    # tc_eq = sf.TimeController(dt=0.1, final_time=5, initial_time=0.0, time_unit="day")

docs.title: Block 21: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Boundary conditions
    time_values = [0*hour,  1*hour]
    nt = len(time_values)

docs.title: Block 22: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    bc_west_salt = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name="West_salt", component=0, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])
    bc_west_ovb = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name = "West_ovb", component=0, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])

docs.title: Block 23: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    bc_east_salt = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name="East_salt", component=0, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])
    bc_east_ovb = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name = "East_ovb", component=0, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])

docs.title: Block 24: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    bc_bottom = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name="Bottom", component=2, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])

docs.title: Block 25: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    bc_south_salt = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name="South_salt", component=1, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])
    bc_south_ovb = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name="South_ovb", component=1, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])

docs.title: Block 26: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
These displacement constraints are expressed component by component. SafeInCave locates the DOFs on the named mesh boundary and pins only the requested component, which is how roller or symmetry conditions are represented without overconstraining the model.

    bc_north_salt = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name="North_salt", component=1, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])
    bc_north_ovb = momBC.DirichletBC(boundary_name="North_ovb", component=1, values=[0.0, 0.0], time_values=[0.0, tc_eq.t_final])

docs.title: Block 27: Extract geometry dimensions
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Extract geometry dimensions
    Lx = grid.Lx
    Ly = grid.Ly
    Lz = grid.Lz
    z_surface = 0.0

docs.title: Block 28: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The mesh is loaded through GridHandlerGMSH, which does more than read coordinates and cells. It also exposes named facet tags for boundary conditions, region tags for material assignment, mesh dimensions, cell volumes, and smoothing operators used when element stresses are reported at nodes or smoothed back to elements.

    g = 9.81
    ovb_thickness, salt_thickness, hanging_wall = get_geometry_parameters(grid_path)
    cavern_roof = ovb_thickness + hanging_wall
    p_roof = 0 + salt_density*g*hanging_wall + ovb_density*g*ovb_thickness

docs.title: Block 29: Pressure at the top of the salt layer (bottom of overburden)
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Pressure at the top of the salt layer (bottom of overburden)
    p_top = ovb_density*g*ovb_thickness

docs.title: Block 30: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
This Neumann condition applies a pressure or traction history. The base value is interpolated in time, and the optional density/reference-position terms add hydrostatic variation along the selected coordinate direction.

    bc_top = momBC.NeumannBC(boundary_name = "Top",
                        direction = 2,
                        density = 0.0,
                        ref_pos = z_surface,
                        values = [0*MPa, 0*MPa],
                        time_values = [0*day,  10*day],
                        g = g_vec[2])

docs.title: Block 31: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
This Neumann condition applies a pressure or traction history. The base value is interpolated in time, and the optional density/reference-position terms add hydrostatic variation along the selected coordinate direction.

    bc_cavern = momBC.NeumannBC(boundary_name = "Cavern",
                        direction = 2,
                        density = gas_density,
                        ref_pos = cavern_roof,
                        values = [0.8*p_roof, 0.8*p_roof],
                        time_values = [0*day,  tc_eq.t_final],
                        g = g_vec[2])

docs.title: Block 32: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    bc_equilibrium = momBC.BcHandler(mom_eq)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_west_salt)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_west_ovb)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_east_salt)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_east_ovb)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_bottom)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_south_salt)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_south_ovb)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_north_salt)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_north_ovb)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_top)
    bc_equilibrium.add_boundary_condition(bc_cavern)

docs.title: Block 33: Set boundary conditions
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    # Set boundary conditions
    mom_eq.set_boundary_conditions(bc_equilibrium)

docs.text:
This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    ouput_folder_equilibrium = os.path.join(output_folder, "equilibrium")

docs.title: Block 35: Print output folder
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Print output folder
    if MPI.COMM_WORLD.rank == 0:
        print(ouput_folder_equilibrium)

docs.title: Block 36: Create output handlers
docs.text:
This path groups all files from the run. SaveFields later creates one XDMF subfolder per registered field, and cavern handlers use the same folder to store fluid-operation histories.

    # Create output handlers
    output_mom = sf.SaveFields(mom_eq)
    output_mom.set_output_folder(ouput_folder_equilibrium)
    output_mom.add_output_field("u", "Displacement (m)")
    output_mom.add_output_field("eps_tot", "Total strain (-)")
    output_mom.add_output_field("sig", "Stress (Pa)")
    output_mom.add_output_field("p_elems", "Mean stress (Pa)")
    output_mom.add_output_field("q_elems", "Von Mises stress (Pa)")
    outputs = [output_mom]

docs.title: Block 37: Define simulator
docs.text:
Simulator_M advances the mechanical problem only. When a cavern handler is supplied, the simulator still updates cavern volumes and pressure boundary loads, but it does not solve a surrounding heat equation.

    # Define simulator
    sim = sf.Simulator_M(mom_eq, tc_eq, outputs, True)
    sim.run()

docs.title: Block 38: Time settings for operation stage
docs.text:
This fixed-step controller sets the operational cadence explicitly. It is useful when the imposed pressure, temperature, or mass-flow schedule should be sampled with a predictable step size.

    # Time settings for operation stage
    tc_op = sf.TimeController(dt=0.5, initial_time=0.0, final_time=240, time_unit="day")

docs.title: Block 39: Define heat diffusion equation
docs.text:
HeatDiffusion allocates the scalar temperature space, cell-wise material fields, UFL measures, and temperature storage used by the thermal solve. The example creates it before assigning material properties because set_material copies those properties into DG0 finite-element fields.

    # Define heat diffusion equation
    heat_eq = sf.HeatDiffusion(grid)

docs.title: Block 40: Define solver
docs.text:
The thermal linear system is solved with PETSc. Conjugate gradients match the symmetric diffusion operator, and the additive Schwarz preconditioner keeps the setup usable in both serial and parallel runs.

    # Define solver
    solver_heat = PETSc.KSP().create(grid.mesh.comm)
    solver_heat.setType("cg")
    solver_heat.getPC().setType("asm")
    solver_heat.setTolerances(rtol=1e-12, max_it=100)
    heat_eq.set_solver(solver_heat)

docs.title: Block 41: Set specific heat capacity
docs.text:
Specific heat capacity controls thermal inertia. SafeInCave stores it on the material and copies it into a DG0 field inside HeatDiffusion, where it multiplies the transient temperature term.

    # Set specific heat capacity
    cp = 850*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_specific_heat_capacity(cp)

docs.title: Block 42: Set thermal conductivity
docs.text:
Thermal conductivity sets the strength of the diffusion operator. Defining it per element keeps the example ready for heterogeneous thermal properties even when the current values are uniform.

    # Set thermal conductivity
    k = 7*to.ones(heat_eq.n_elems, dtype=to.float64)
    mat.set_thermal_conductivity(k)

docs.title: Block 43: Set material properties to heat_equation
docs.text:
Attaching the material to HeatDiffusion copies conductivity, density, and heat capacity into finite-element fields used by the thermal variational form.

    # Set material properties to heat_equation
    heat_eq.set_material(mat)

docs.title: Block 44: Set initial temperature
docs.text:
The initial temperature initializes both current and previous thermal states inside HeatDiffusion. Without this step the transient solve would not have a physically meaningful starting field.

    # Set initial temperature
    T0_field_nodes = create_field_nodes(grid, T_field_fun)
    heat_eq.set_initial_T(T0_field_nodes)

docs.title: Block 45: Define boundary conditions for heat diffusion
docs.text:
This small block connects the surrounding setup steps and is retained so the annotated listing remains complete and in the same order as main.py.

    # Define boundary conditions for heat diffusion
    time_values = [tc_op.t_initial, tc_op.t_final]
    nt = len(time_values)

docs.title: Block 46: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.

    bc_handler = heatBC.BcHandler(heat_eq)

docs.title: Block 47: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
This Dirichlet condition fixes temperature on a named boundary. The values are time-interpolated by the heat BcHandler, which turns the user schedule into DOLFINx essential boundary conditions at each step.

    bc_top = heatBC.DirichletBC("Top", nt*[T_top], time_values)
    bc_bottom = heatBC.NeumannBC("Bottom", nt*[dTdZ], time_values)
    bc_east_salt = heatBC.NeumannBC("East_salt", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_east_ovb = heatBC.NeumannBC("East_ovb", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_west_salt = heatBC.NeumannBC("West_salt", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_west_ovb = heatBC.NeumannBC("West_ovb", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_south_salt = heatBC.NeumannBC("South_salt", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_south_ovb = heatBC.NeumannBC("South_ovb", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_north_salt = heatBC.NeumannBC("North_salt", nt*[0.0], time_values)
    bc_north_ovb = heatBC.NeumannBC("North_ovb", nt*[0.0], time_values)

docs.title: Block 48: Continuation of the script
docs.text:
The boundary handler is the bridge between simple Python boundary objects and the assembled variational problem. It stores each condition by type, updates time-dependent values, and supplies the forms or DOF constraints needed by the solver.
